newsitem.title: ITALY: Pope making smooth recovery after operation.
newsitem.headline: Pope making smooth recovery after operation.

text.p: Pope John Paul was making a smooth recovery from an appendix operation on Wednesday, walking in corridors and chatting with doctors who said a definitive biopsy showed that he did not have a tumour.
"He spoke with us and he strolled around the corridors of his suite," Professor Luigi Ortona, a senior member of the Pope's medical team at the Gemelli hospital, told Reuters.
"Everything is fine," Ortona said.
An official medical bulletin later confirmed that the post-operative phase was proceeding well.
It said that the Pope, 76, had no fever or pain. His blood pressure, heart rate, breathing and other vital signs were normal. The Pontiff had also begun taking liquid food.
The statement said final tests of tissue removed during surgery had confirmed the findings of initial post-operative analysis that no new tumour was present.
Tuesday morning's 50-minute operation was accompanied by intense media speculation that the Pope might have another tumour. He had a colon tumour the size of an orange removed in 1992.
Two days of comforting medical bulletins, however, have done little to deflect media attention from what independent doctors say may be the Pope's affliction with Parkinson's Disease.
The Polish-born Pontiff's left hand trembles, sometimes violently and uncontrollably, and he appears to suffer from facial muscle rigidity and a stooped, slow gait.

At a news conference on Tuesday following the operation, Professor Francesco Crucitti, the chief surgeon, sidestepped a barrage of questions about whether the Pope has Parkinson's or a related neurological disorder.

"There are specialists who are following him. This is not my field," Crucitti said. His reference to specialists appeared to be the first public official indication from a member of the Pope's medical team that his symptoms are being monitored.

Asked to elaborate on Crucitti's comment, a well-placed medical source at the hospital said on Wednesday: "We are trying to do everything possibile to favour the positive evolution of this situation."
Other sources said that doctors would concentrate on post-operative care during the Pope's stay at the hospital, expected to last for seven days.
But doctors are talking more openly, albeit generically, about the problem.
"Neurology is not my specialisation," papal anaesthetist Corrado Manni said, adding that people should not connect such trembling with a possible decline in mental abilities.
"Parkinson's Disease is one thing, Alzheimer's Disease is another," said Manni. Alzheimer's is a progressive degenerative ailment that impairs memory, thinking and behaviour.
Doctors have been advising the Pope to slow down.
"If I could venture my own opinion, I think the Pope should rest more," Crucitti said. Manni added: "The Pope is made of strong stuff but he should work a little less."
But all indications are that the Pope, who aides say gets bored when he is not active, will disobey doctors as he has after past operations and resume a punishing schedule.

"I believe that the Pope will lead us to the great Jubilee of the year 2000," said Cardinal Jozef Glemp, the Polish primate. "His thoughts and pastoral preparations are all aimed at this date and he intends to see them to fruition."
